zh: 要数的是 s2 中下标 i<j<k 的三元组，使三个字符依次等于 s1，不同下标算不同方案。三重枚举太慢，但 s1 只有 3 个字符，可以按“已经匹配到 s1 的前几个字符”来计数。
从左往右扫描 s2，维护 one、two、three，分别表示已扫描部分中匹配 s1 前 1、2、3 个字符的子序列个数。当前字符可以作为某个前缀匹配的最后一个字符，接在短一位的匹配后面。
对每个字符依次判断：等于 s1 第三个字符时 three 加上 two，等于第二个字符时 two 加上 one，等于第一个字符时 one 加 1。必须按这个从长到短的顺序更新，否则 s1 含重复字母时同一个字符会被用两次。答案最大约 2×10^16，要用 64 位整数，不能用浮点。
en: Count index triples i<j<k in s2 whose characters spell s1 in order, where different indices count separately. A triple loop is too slow, but s1 has only 3 characters, so count by how many leading characters of s1 have been matched.

Scan s2 from left to right with counters one, two and three: the numbers of subsequences in the scanned part matching the first 1, 2 and 3 characters of s1. The current character can end a match of some prefix by extending a match one character shorter.

For each character: if it equals the third character of s1, add two to three; if it equals the second, add one to two; if it equals the first, add 1 to one. Update in exactly this order, from longest to shortest, or a repeated letter in s1 would let one character be used twice. The answer reaches about 2×10^16, so use 64-bit integers, never floating point.

explanationEn:
## Fixed source and numeric type disclosure

fastprep/Morgan Stanley/stanley-get-subsequence-count.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc fully specifies: s1 has length exactly 3, 1≤|s2|≤500000, and both strings contain only A to Z. Count the number of times s1 occurs as a subsequence of s2; all three original examples explicitly list distinct 1-based index triples. Therefore counting is by index choice, not deduplicated by the resulting characters, and not limited to contiguous substrings. All three original examples are kept.

The raw return description and the starter say int, but the original length range allows results far beyond 32 bits; in web/content/docs/companies/morgan-stanley.mdx at the same fixed commit, the Java implementation explicitly returns long, the C++ one explicitly returns long long, and Python keeps exact integers. This site outputs the exact decimal integer of the mathematical count, without a modulus, without truncation, and without shrinking the input range. The full paths and fingerprints of both sources are recorded separately. Standard input is two lines of strings; no upstream code was executed.

## Approach

Scan s2 from left to right, maintaining one, two, and three: the numbers of subsequences in the scanned part that equal the first 1, 2, and 3 characters of s1. When the current character equals s1[2], add two to three; when it equals s1[1], add one to two; when it equals s1[0], add 1 to one. The three conditions are independent, and the updates must go from the longest prefix to the shortest, so that when s1 contains repeated letters the current character is not used more than once in the same subsequence.

## Proof of correctness

Assume the three counts are correct before processing the current index. For the target prefix of length j, all matching subsequences fall into two classes: those that do not choose the current character, whose number is the existing count; and those that choose the current character as their last element, which is possible only when it equals the j-th target character, and whose number is exactly the count of matches of the length j−1 prefix formed before it. The two classes have disjoint index sets and together cover all matches.

Updating in the reverse order j=3, 2, 1, the shorter-prefix count read each time does not yet include the current index, so every new subsequence has strictly increasing indices. The initial empty text has no non-empty match and all three counts are 0, which matches the base of the induction. Hence after the full scan, three counts all valid index triples and only those. When the length is less than 3 the answer is naturally 0, so the source's input range does not need to be shrunk.

## Complexity and the 64-bit bound

The scan takes O(|s2|) time with O(1) counting state; reading standard input as a whole takes O(|s2|) space. Every match corresponds to a distinct combination of three indices, so the answer is at most C(|s2|,3), which over the full range is at most C(500000,3)=20833208333500000. This exceeds the 32-bit bound and the JavaScript safe-integer bound, but is below the signed 64-bit bound 9223372036854775807. one and two are at most 500000 and C(500000,2) respectively, which is equally safe. Python uses exact integers; other languages should use 64 bits and must not convert values to floating point midway.

## Independent verification and full boundaries

The small oracle directly enumerates the three indices i<j<k and compares character by character, without the prefix DP. 163 unique inputs were cross-checked against the real reference program run as a subprocess. The formal full-length cases are additionally counted by their closed-form structure and cross-checked with a linear method that enumerates the middle index and multiplies the left and right match counts: AAA against all A gives C(500000,3); ABC against blocks gives the product of the three block lengths; (ABC)^q followed by AB gives C(q+2,3); ABA against (AB)^m gives Σj(m−j)=C(m+1,3). The tests also cover the repeated targets AAB and ABB, no match, lengths 1/2, and exact results beyond 32 bits and beyond the safe floating-point range. Large counts in the expected outputs and in the verification records are all stored as decimal strings. The two negative controls exit normally and are rejected, one for updating in forward order and one for 32-bit overflow.
